The Epic of Gilgamesh. Humanity's oldest known work of literature, composed in ancient Sumeria around the twenty-one hundreds BCE. It recounts the adventures of Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk, and his companion Enkidu, exploring themes of friendship, mortality, and the human search for immortality.

This ancient epic was composed in cuneiform on clay tablets, originally in Sumerian, later transcribed into Akkadian, and preserved across multiple copies and versions spanning centuries. The narrative was initially orally transmitted before being written down, reflecting the epic traditions of Mesopotamian storytelling and theology. The story centers on Gilgamesh, the tyrannical king of Uruk—a historical figure who ruled around twenty-seven fifty BCE—who becomes humanized through his friendship with the wild man Enkidu. It chronicles their journey together through adventures including the defeat of the monster Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, sent by the goddess Ishtar. When Enkidu dies, this traumatizes Gilgamesh and drives him to seek a path to eternal life and wisdom from Utnapishtim, the immortal survivor of the flood. The epic features a flood narrative, an earlier version of similar stories found in later Mesopotamian and biblical texts, suggesting a shared cultural memory of catastrophic flooding. Throughout, the text explores fundamental human concerns: mortality, friendship, the futility of seeking immortality, and the dignity of accepting one's fate as a human. The epic concludes with Gilgamesh's acceptance of human mortality and his return to rule Uruk with new perspective and wisdom, the true treasure he gained from his journey. The text was preserved in the Ashurbanipal library at Nineveh, dating to the seventh century BCE, allowing its survival to the modern era and making it accessible to scholars through the collected royal archives. The eleven-tablet Standard Babylonian version, discovered in Nineveh in eighteen seventy-two, became the primary source for understanding this foundational work of world literature. The epic connects to the Akkadian empire, in which it was preserved and propagated, the Assyrian empire where copies were discovered in Ashurbanipal's royal library in Nineveh, Sumerian civilization as the origin of its composition, Mesopotamia where the story is set and reflects the region's cosmology and values, the ancient flood narrative of which it contains one of history's oldest versions, and Mesopotamian religion, which the epic depicts with gods like Inanna and Shamash intervening in mortal affairs.
